what: Waystar provides software that handles healthcare billing. Hospitals and medical practices use it to check a patient’s insurance, submit claims, chase denied claims, and collect payments — the administrative work between treating a patient and being paid for it.
customers: Hospitals, health systems, physician groups and other healthcare providers in the United States, who pay based on the volume of claims and payments processed.
money: Recurring software fees scaled to claims and payment volume processed.
moat: American healthcare billing is extraordinarily complicated — thousands of payers with different rules, codes and denial patterns — and a provider’s revenue depends on getting it right. Once Waystar is processing a hospital’s claims, it is embedded in the cash collection process, which nobody disrupts voluntarily. Revenue also scales with claim volume rather than headcount.
risks: Debt of $1.5B against $86.2M of cash is substantial, a legacy of the private equity ownership that preceded the listing.
Reported net income of $135.2M gives a price/earnings ratio of 39.3, which assumes continued growth.
Hospital IT budgets are under pressure, and providers consolidate vendors when money is tight.
Any simplification of American healthcare billing would reduce the problem Waystar exists to solve, though that has never happened.
Twenty-two analysts average a $34.82 target against a $27.09 price, a 29% gap.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $704.9M in 2022 to $1.1B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $1.3B.
Free cash flow of $264.1M on $1.3B of revenue is strong, and the shares trade at about 19.7 times it.
Revenue scales with claim volume rather than with the number of users, which is efficient growth.
Being embedded in a hospital’s cash collection makes the product extremely difficult to remove.
Healthcare claim volumes grow with an ageing population regardless of the economy.
watch: Net revenue retention and claim volume growth. The business grows with the volume flowing through it, and retention tells you whether hospitals are expanding their use.
view: Waystar exists because American healthcare billing is a mess, and it is worth appreciating the scale of that mess. A hospital submits claims to thousands of different insurers, each with its own rules, codes, documentation requirements and denial patterns. Getting it wrong means not being paid, or being paid late, which for a hospital running on thin margins is an existential matter. Software that navigates this reliably is not a convenience; it is part of the cash collection apparatus.

That produces unusually good business characteristics. Revenue scales with the volume of claims and payments processed rather than with headcount, so growth does not require proportionally more cost. The product is embedded in the revenue cycle, which nobody rips out voluntarily — a failed billing migration means a hospital stops getting paid. And claim volumes grow with an ageing population regardless of the economy.

The complication is the balance sheet: $1.5 billion of debt against $86 million of cash, left over from the private equity ownership that preceded the listing. That is a lot of fixed cost ahead of the equity, and it is why a business generating $264 million of free cash flow still reports only $135 million of net income. The reported 39.3 times price/earnings ratio reflects interest expense, not an expensive business; 19.7 times free cash flow is the honest figure.

The theoretical risk people raise is that American healthcare billing gets simplified, which would shrink the problem Waystar solves. I would weight that at close to zero — every attempt in forty years has added complexity rather than removed it. The real risk is more mundane: hospital IT budgets are tight, providers consolidate vendors when money is short, and a competitor bundling billing into a broader platform could win on price. Net revenue retention and claim volume growth are the two numbers that show whether that is happening.
bull: Claim volumes grow with an ageing population, hospitals expand their use of an embedded billing system, and debt reduction lifts a 20 times free cash flow multiple.
bear: Hospital IT budgets tighten and providers consolidate vendors, growth slows, and $1.5 billion of debt leaves little room for a soft patch.
